sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Every Go project uses modules, and understanding go.mod is a prerequisite for working in any Go codebase. Fresher interviews include module questions because adding a dependency, running `go mod tidy`, and understanding what go.sum is for are things you will do on your first day. Getting these wrong signals you have only worked in isolated tutorials, not real team projects.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Two files, two roles:

- **`go.mod` is the dependency declaration** — it says what your module is called and what other modules it needs (and at what version). Think of it like `package.json` in Node.js or `pom.xml` in Maven — human-edited, committed to source control.
- **`go.sum` is the cryptographic lock file** — it records the exact hash of every dependency version. You never edit it manually; `go get` and `go mod tidy` maintain it. Always commit go.sum — it lets anyone reproduce the exact same build.
- **The module path is also the import path prefix.** If your module is `github.com/alice/myapp`, then a file at `internal/config/config.go` is imported as `"github.com/alice/myapp/internal/config"`. This is how Go imports work — they are URLs, not relative paths.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **go.mod and module** — `module github.com/yourname/myapp` declares the module path; `go 1.21` sets the minimum Go version; `require` section lists direct dependencies
- **Packages and imports** — each directory is one package; `package main` is the entry point; import path = module path + directory relative path
- **Exported vs unexported** — identifiers starting with a capital letter are exported (public); lowercase are unexported (package-private); this applies to types, functions, variables, methods, struct fields
- **go get** — `go get github.com/gin-gonic/gin@v1.9.1` adds a dependency and updates go.mod and go.sum; `go get` with no version gets the latest tagged release
- **go mod tidy** — removes dependencies in go.mod that are no longer imported; adds dependencies that are imported but missing; always run before committing
- **go.sum** — contains checksums for every dependency at every version used; ensures reproducible builds; always commit to source control
- **Module path convention** — typically a VCS URL (`github.com/org/repo`); for internal projects, a domain you control (`mycompany.internal/myapp`); must not start with a version suffix unless it is v2+

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **go.mod vs go.sum** — `go.mod` is the dependency list (you edit it); `go.sum` is the integrity hash (the toolchain manages it). Interviewers ask this directly. A wrong answer reveals you have not worked with modules hands-on.
- **Unexported fields and JSON** — lowercase struct fields are not only package-private, they are invisible to `encoding/json`. This is the most common connection between modules/packages and JSON that appears in interviews.
- **`go mod tidy` before committing** — if you add an import but do not run `go mod tidy`, the build on another machine will fail. The command to run is `go mod tidy && go build ./...` before every commit.
- **v2+ modules need a major version suffix** — `module github.com/alice/mylib/v2` — the path must end in `/v2`. Importing it requires `import "github.com/alice/mylib/v2/config"`. This trips freshers who see the suffix in the wild and do not know why.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"`go.mod` declares what my module is and what it depends on — I add dependencies with `go get` and run `go mod tidy` before committing to clean up unused ones. `go.sum` is the cryptographic hash of every dependency version; I always commit it so the build is reproducible on any machine. In Go, every capitalised identifier is exported and every lowercase one is package-private — there is no `public`/`private` keyword, just the capitalisation of the first letter."*
